activities.caption: fill the blanks — the pocket that does the work
activities.name: enSiteCloze

config.text: Every enzyme has an active site — a small pocket formed by the protein's precise 3-D folding, typically involving just %%0%% to %%1%% amino acid side chains. The classic description is %%2%%; the modern refinement is %%3%% fit — the enzyme moulds around the substrate, straining its bonds toward breaking.
config.hint: Only a substrate whose shape and chemical groups complement the pocket fits — which is why enzymes are specific.

activities.caption: true or false — reading Vmax and Km
activities.name: enKmJudge

statements.s: Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate reaches exactly half of Vmax.
statements.why: That is its definition — a genuine physical constant of the enzyme–substrate pair.
It is an affinity figure, not a rate figure — the two numbers answer different questions.

statements.s: An enzyme can grip tightly (low Km) yet turn over slowly (modest Vmax).
statements.why: Or grip loosely and work furiously — which is why drug design targets them separately.

statements.s: Vmax is reached when every active site is occupied and extra substrate stops mattering.
statements.why: The flattening of the curve is saturation.

activities.caption: same chemistry, different optimum — drag to the hot spring
activities.name: enTempCompare

config.prompt: The temperature dial, two settings — drag the divider:

before.label: human-typical enzyme
before.text: Peaks near 37–40 °C; the folded shape is held by weak bonds — hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions — that extra heat shakes apart.

after.label: thermophile (Taq)
after.text: Thermus aquaticus lives at 70 °C and its DNA polymerase survives the 95 °C of a PCR machine — the whole biotech industry runs on it.

config.why: Same chemistry, different optimum — that is what adapting a protein's weak bonds means in practice.

activities.anchor: Pepsin in the stomach has an optimum near pH 2
activities.caption: pair each enzyme with its pH address
activities.name: enPhMatch

config.prompt: pH matters because catalytic side chains depend on protonation — pair each enzyme with its working pH:

pairs.left: haemoglobin and every enzyme of respiration
pairs.right: pH-tuned to blood's 7.4, buffered within 0.05 units

config.why: Move one or two pH units from the optimum and activity collapses — the side chains gain or lose protons and can no longer form the right interactions.

activities.anchor: Amylase digesting starch can be tracked by sampling drops into iodine
activities.caption: rebuild the rate-measurement protocol
activities.name: enPracticalOrder

config.prompt: The staple practical, done properly — put the protocol in order:
items: Pick something you can watch, and hold everything else constant
Run a boiled-enzyme control to prove the reaction you see is really catalysis
Time the initial rate — the first few seconds or minutes
Repeat at each temperature or pH to plot the curves properly
config.why: Late measurements mix enzyme performance with substrate shortage — measuring the initial rate is exactly the confusion the Michaelis–Menten framework avoids.

activities.anchor: Many enzymes also refuse to work alone
activities.caption: file the helpers by what they are
activities.name: enCofactorBuckets

config.prompt: The protein provides shape and specificity; the partner provides chemistry. File each helper:

items.label: coenzyme A carrying acetyl groups into the Krebs cycle
vitamin B₁ — no coenzyme, no working decarboxylase
the iron-containing haem bound permanently in catalase

config.why: Vitamins are coenzyme precursors — which is why a dietary deficiency can stall one specific metabolic step and, in B₁'s case, fail the nervous system.

config.prompt: End-product inhibition, step by step — put the loop in order:
items: Isoleucine builds up in the cell
Some binds an allosteric site on threonine deaminase — the pathway's first enzyme
The enzyme is forced into an inactive shape
Isoleucine is consumed, and the inhibition lifts
config.why: Control the first enzyme of a pathway and the whole line stops cheaply — allosteric regulation switches pathways without touching the genes.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the drug spec sheet
activities.name: enDrugSpot

config.prompt: This pharmacology answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Statins competitively block HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.
Aspirin permanently disables COX enzymes, cutting inflammatory prostaglandins.
Penicillin jamms the transpeptidase that cross-links bacterial cell walls.
Cyanide poisons cytochrome c oxidase — cells that cannot use oxygen, internal suffocation.
Most medicines work by supplying the energy a stalled enzyme needs.
config.correction: Medicines mostly BLOCK or JAM enzymes — enzymes supply no energy; they lower activation energy, and inhibitors stop them.
config.why: Pharmacology is enzyme interference with a spec sheet: block, disable, jamm, poison — never 'energise'.
